title: Mass & Energy Analysis of Control Volumes

questions.prompt: Why does **enthalpy** (not internal energy) appear in flow-system energy balances?
choices: Flow work $Pv$ combines with $u$ into $h = u + Pv$
Internal energy is zero for flowing fluids
It's a historical convention with no physical basis
questions.explanation: Pushing fluid across the boundary takes flow work $Pv$ per unit mass; bundling it with $u$ gives enthalpy — so streams carry $h + V^2/2 + gz$.

questions.prompt: **Steady-flow** operation means…
choices: Properties at every point in the control volume are constant in time
The fluid moves at constant velocity everywhere
Mass accumulates at a steady rate
questions.explanation: Nothing changes with time inside the control volume: $dm_{cv}/dt = 0$ and $dE_{cv}/dt = 0$ — so mass in = mass out and energy in = energy out.

questions.prompt: Across an ideal **throttling valve**, which property is conserved?
questions.explanation: No work, no heat, negligible KE/PE → $h_1 = h_2$. Pressure drops sharply, temperature usually drops, and entropy *increases*.

questions.prompt: Which device converts a flow's **enthalpy into kinetic energy** with no work or heat transfer?
questions.explanation: A nozzle accelerates the flow: $h_1 + V_1^2/2 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$ — enthalpy drops, velocity rises. A diffuser does the reverse.

questions.prompt: For an **adiabatic turbine** with negligible $\Delta KE$ and $\Delta PE$, the SFEE reduces to…
questions.explanation: With $\dot Q \approx 0$ and KE/PE dropped, the enthalpy drop becomes shaft work out: $\dot W = \dot m(h_1 - h_2) > 0$ for a turbine.

questions.prompt: Saturated-liquid refrigerant passes through an expansion valve. At the exit you expect…
choices: Lower pressure, lower temperature, partly vaporized
Lower pressure, same temperature, still all liquid
Lower pressure, higher temperature, all vapor
questions.explanation: Throttling keeps $h$ constant while $P$ drops; part of the liquid flashes to vapor and the temperature falls to the new $T_{sat}$ — the heart of refrigeration.

questions.prompt: Solve the mass-flow relation $\dot m = \rho V A$ for the **velocity**:
questions.explanation: Divide by $\rho A$. Equivalently $V = \dot m\,v/A$ when you're given specific volume instead of density.

questions.prompt: For an adiabatic nozzle (no work, $\Delta pe \approx 0$), the exit velocity is…
questions.explanation: From $h_1 + V_1^2/2 = h_2 + V_2^2/2$, solve for $V_2$ — with $h$ in **J/kg** so the units match $V^2$.

questions.prompt: The work per unit mass to pump an (incompressible) **liquid** from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is approximately…
questions.explanation: For a liquid, $v$ is nearly constant, so $\Delta h \approx v\Delta P$ — no property tables needed.

questions.prompt: Water ($\rho = 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$) flows at **2.0 m/s** through a pipe of area **0.005 m²**. Find $\dot m$.
questions.explanation: $\dot m = \rho V A = 1000 \times 2.0 \times 0.005 = 10$ kg/s.

questions.prompt: Steam flows through an adiabatic turbine at $\dot m = 4.0\ \text{kg/s}$, entering at $h_1 = 3000$ and leaving at $h_2 = 2400\ \text{kJ/kg}$. Find the power output.
A pump raises water ($v = 0.001\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$) from **100 kPa** to **3000 kPa**. Find the pump work per kg.
For a **single-stream steady-flow** device, the mass balance requires…
choices: Mass to accumulate in the device
questions.explanation: Steady state means no mass accumulates, so the inlet and outlet mass-flow rates are equal.

questions.prompt: The **flow work** per unit mass needed to push fluid across a boundary is…
questions.explanation: Flow work is $Pv$; combined with internal energy it forms enthalpy, $h = u + Pv$ — why $h$ appears in flow equations.

questions.prompt: A **diffuser** (no work, adiabatic)…
choices: Slows the flow and raises its enthalpy
Speeds the flow and lowers its enthalpy
Adds shaft work to the flow
questions.explanation: A diffuser is a nozzle in reverse: kinetic energy converts back to enthalpy, so velocity drops and $h$ rises.

questions.prompt: Which steady-flow device is characterized by $h_1 = h_2$?
questions.explanation: A throttle has no work, no heat and negligible KE/PE, so enthalpy is conserved — the defining isenthalpic device.

questions.prompt: Solve $\dot m = VA/v$ for the flow **area** $A$:
questions.explanation: Rearranged continuity: $A = \dot m v / V$ — used for sizing pipe or nozzle cross-sections.

questions.prompt: For an adiabatic **compressor** (negligible KE/PE), the power input is…
questions.explanation: A compressor raises enthalpy, so the input work is $\dot m(h_2 - h_1)$ — the reverse of the turbine form.

questions.prompt: Steam enters an adiabatic nozzle at **20 m/s** and its enthalpy drops by **15 kJ/kg**. Find the exit velocity, in m/s.
A pump raises water ($v = 0.001\ \text{m}^3/\text{kg}$) from **200 kPa** to **4000 kPa** at $\dot m = 5.0\ \text{kg/s}$. Find the pump power, in kW.
